title: Spectral Gap Governs Eigenvalue Resolvability in Quantum Phase Estimation: Spectral Features Versus a Physical Baseline
content: Can simple spectral properties of a quantum gate, computed classically from its eigenvalues, predict how well quantum phase estimation (QPE) performs on that gate? We study three spectral features, a normalised Spectral Coherence Metric (SCM), the spectral gap, and a circular phase spread, using ideal Qiskit Aer simulations of 1,756 two-qubit gates (1,000 Haar-random unitaries plus three controlled spectral classes) for m = 3, 4, 5 ancilla qubits and three independent random seeds. All prediction targets are measured from simulated QPE circuits. When QPE is run on single eigenstates, the spectral features have no predictive power for the estimation error (cross-validated R2 ≤ 0), because that error is fixed by the position of each eigenphase on the 2m-point measurement grid. When the target register is prepared in an equal superposition of eigenvectors, the spectral features do predict eigenvalue resolvability, the fraction of eigenphases that appear as separate peaks: for Haar-random gates with m = 4, a random forest reaches R2 = 0.633 ± 0.020, and the spectral gap dominates the feature importance (0.88). However, a parameter-light physical baseline that counts gaps larger than a multiple of the grid spacing 2π/2m matches the learned models in accuracy and exceeds them in balanced accuracy (0.78 versus at most 0.63). We conclude that spectral structure, through the spectral gap, governs resolvability in superposition-input QPE in the way expected from the standard resolution limit, and that machine learning adds little beyond this physical rule.
